Here is the complete, itemized extraction from James W. Aageson’s doctoral dissertation (Paul's Use of Scripture, Oxford University, 1983) for each of the 12 B001 target passages, systematically addressing the requested analytical criteria.
1. B001-1: Romans 4:3 / Genesis 15:6
Expresses Uncertainty / Allows Oral Transmission or Quotation from Memory: Aageson notes that the word order of ἐπίστευσεν and Ἀβραάμ is transposed between Romans 4:3 (Ἐπίστευσεν δὲ Ἀβραὰμ τῷ θεῷ) and Galatians 3:6 (Ἀβραὰμ ἐπίστευσεν). He explicitly acknowledges that while this does not affect the underlying sense, "the possibility cannot be ruled out that Paul in some cases may have quoted from memory" or exhibited minor quotational inconsistency
1
.
Discusses Competing Textual Form & Authorial Adaptation: Aageson highlights that in the double citation of Genesis 15:6, the particle δέ is included in Romans 4:3 but omitted in Galatians 3:6 (neither contains δέ in LXX Genesis 15:6). He classifies this as a minor literary/stylistic adaptation designed by Paul to integrate the quotation smoothly into the epistolary sentence
1
.
Disagrees with Another Scholar / Traditional Interpretation: Aageson notes that Paul’s exegesis in Romans 4:3 relies on the chronological narrative sequence of Genesis 15:6 (faith reckoned as righteousness) prior to Genesis 17 (circumcision). He points out that Paul uses this sequence to extract a principle of faith-righteousness vs. works-righteousness that runs counter to traditional Tannaitic/rabbinic interpretations of Abraham’s accumulated merit
1
2
.
2. B001-2: Romans 9:25 / Hosea 2:23 [LXX 2:25]
Discusses Competing Textual Form: Aageson analyzes the textual traditions of Hosea 2:23 (25), pointing out that Paul in Romans 9:25 aligns with Codex Vaticanus (LXX-B) in using love terminology (ἀγαπήσω / ἠγαπημένην), whereas Codex Alexandrinus (LXX-A) reads mercy terminology (ἐλεήσω / ἠλεημένην)
1
3
.
Allows Authorial Adaptation, Oral Transmission, or Unknown Textual Form: Aageson notes that Paul substitutes καλέσω for LXX ἐρῶ (καὶ ἐρῶ τῷ Οὐ λαῷ μου). Regarding the unique word sequence in Romans 9:25, Aageson states that it is at variance with LXX-A, LXX-B, and all major manuscripts. He writes that "the lack of a clear hermeneutical reason for the variations, except perhaps for emphasis, suggests that they are either the result of Paul's fidelity to a variant tradition or the result of his lack of precision in quoting" from memory
1
3
.
Acknowledges Evidence That Weakens Preferred Interpretation: Although Aageson prefers the view that Paul intentionally substituted καλέσω to create a deliberate verbal catchword tally (gezerah shawah) with κληθήσονται in Hosea 1:10 (Romans 9:26) and ἐκάλεσεν in Romans 9:24, he explicitly admits that "the possibility that the parallel members have been transposed because of Paul's inaccurate quoting from memory cannot be excluded"
1
3
.
Disagrees with Another Scholar: Aageson addresses Nils Dahl’s proposal that Hosea 2:23 refers to both Jews and Gentiles simultaneously; Aageson disputes this framing, arguing that "it is more consistent with Paul's argument in Rom. 9... that 9:25-26 refers to the Gentiles and 9:27-29 to Israel"
4
.
3. B001-3: Romans 9:26 / Hosea 1:10 [LXX 2:1]
Discusses Competing Textual Form: Aageson points out that Romans 9:26 agrees directly with Codex Alexandrinus (LXX-A) against Codex Vaticanus (LXX-B) by prefixing ἐκεῖ to κληθήσονται (pr εκει A) and omitting καὶ αὐτοί (om και αυτοι A), yielding ἐκεῖ κληθήσονται υἱοὶ θεοῦ ζῶντος
1
3
.
Notes Hebrew/Greek Ambiguity & Marginal Versions: Aageson notes that the margin of Codex Marchalianus (Qmg) records that Symmachus and Theodotion (s' θ') likewise omitted τὸ καί
1
3
.
Expresses Uncertainty / Allows Unknown Textual Form: Aageson acknowledges uncertainty as to whether ἐκεῖ was already present in Paul’s underlying Greek manuscript (as reflected in LXX-A) or whether Paul personally inserted ἐκεῖ to strengthen the locative emphasis
1
3
.
4. B001-4: Romans 10:11 / Isaiah 28:16
Discusses Competing Textual Form: Aageson notes that ἐπʼ αὐτῷ is present in LXX-A, Codex Sinaiticus, and Paul’s citations (Romans 9:33 and 10:11), but is omitted in LXX-B
1
3
.
Allows Authorial Adaptation / Catchword Influence: Aageson highlights that Paul inserts πᾶς in Romans 10:11 (Πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων...), whereas he omitted πᾶς when quoting the exact same verse in Romans 9:33 (ὁ πιστεύων...). Aageson states that πᾶς was added in Romans 10:11 due to the verbal catchword influence of πᾶς in Joel 2:32 (quoted two verses later in Rom 10:13)
1
3
.
Disagrees with Another Scholar: Aageson disputes C.K. Barrett’s interpretation that the "stone of stumbling" in Romans 9:32–33 / 10:11 refers primarily to the Mosaic Law. Aligning with C.E.B. Cranfield, Aageson argues that the "stone" refers christologically to Christ
1
5
.
Acknowledges Evidence That Weakens Preferred Interpretation: Aageson examines C.H. Dodd’s "testimony hypothesis" (which claims Paul copied from a fixed, pre-existing Christian testimony collection combining Isa 28:16 and Isa 8:14). While Aageson acknowledges the striking verbal similarities between Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6–8, he points out that 1 Peter includes Psalm 118:22 and omits Isaiah 8:14, demonstrating that Paul adapted early traditions for his own argument rather than mechanically copying a fixed testimonia sheet
1
unfold_less
2
5
.
5. B001-5: Romans 10:13 / Joel 2:32 [LXX 3:5]
Disagrees with Another Scholar / Allows Oral or Liturgical Transmission: Aageson compares Paul’s citation of Joel 3:5 LXX in Romans 10:13 with Peter’s speech in Acts 2:21. He explicitly disagrees with views that Paul merely adopted an early Church Pentecost tradition, stating: "If Joel 3:1-5 had come to be understood in the early church primarily as a prophecy about Pentecost, it is evident that Paul has not used 3:5 in conformity with this tradition. It would appear that verbal and specific thematic considerations [πᾶς and ἐπικαλέω] have informed Paul's use of this text in Romans and not a Pentecost tradition"
1
5
.
Authorial Adaptation: Aageson notes that Paul inserts γάρ into Joel 3:5 LXX (Πᾶς γὰρ ὃς ἂν...) for syntactical integration and epistolary transition
1
3
.
6. B001-6: Romans 11:34 / Isaiah 40:13
Discusses Competing Textual Form: Aageson notes that Paul and LXX-A read the word order σύμβουλος αὐτοῦ in both Romans 11:34 and 1 Corinthians 2:16, whereas LXX-B transposes the terms (αὐτοῦ σύμβουλος)
1
3
.
Allows Authorial Adaptation / Selective Quotation: Aageson highlights that Paul quotes different clauses of Isaiah 40:13 in Romans 11:34 (Isa 40:13a–b) and 1 Corinthians 2:16 (Isa 40:13a, c), demonstrating Paul’s freedom to select and adapt distinct portions of the same scriptural passage to fit different epistolary contexts
1
3
.
7. B001-7: Romans 15:12 / Isaiah 11:10
Allows Authorial Adaptation / Minor Omission: Aageson observes that Paul omits the introductory temporal clause ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ from Isaiah 11:10 LXX when quoting it in Romans 15:12. He categorizes this as a minor, non-substantial stylistic adjustment
1
3
.
Discusses Pre-Pauline Tradition: Aageson discusses Dietrich-Alex Koch’s argument that Isaiah 11:10 belonged to a pre-Pauline christological catena. He shows how Paul integrates it into his four-verse catena in Romans 15:9–12 through the verbal catchword ἔθνη
1
unfold_less
3
5
.
8. B001-8: 1 Corinthians 1:19 / Isaiah 29:14
Discusses Competing Textual Form / Authorial Substitution: Aageson notes that Paul substitutes ἀθετήσω ("I will set aside/confound") for LXX κρύψω ("I will hide") in the second clause (καὶ τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν συνετῶν κρύψω)
1
3
.
Disagrees with Another Scholar: Aageson discusses E. Earle Ellis’s hypothesis that 1 Corinthians 1:18–31 was an independent, pre-Pauline Jewish-Christian midrashic unit adopted by Paul. Aageson argues that even if pre-Pauline material was present, Isaiah 29:14 actively functions as the verbal and thematic catalyst generating Paul’s own exposition on God rendering foolish the wisdom of the world
1
unfold_less
3
5
.
9. B001-9: 1 Corinthians 6:16 / Genesis 2:24
Discusses Competing Textual Form & Authorial Adaptation: Comparing Paul’s double citation of Genesis 2:24 in 1 Corinthians 6:16 and Ephesians 5:31, Aageson points out that 1 Corinthians 6:16 inserts the parenthetical formula γάρ, φησίν (Ἔσονται γάρ, φησίν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν). He states this formula was added purely for syntactical sentence integration
1
3
.
Allows Minor Textual Omission: Aageson notes that Ephesians 5:31 omits αὐτοῦ after πατέρα and μητέρα, which he classifies as a minor stylistic dropping of unnecessary pronouns
1
3
.
10. B001-10: 1 Corinthians 9:9 / Deuteronomy 25:4
Discusses Competing Textual Form / Lexical Variant: Aageson notes that 1 Corinthians 9:9 reads κημώσεις ("you shall not muzzle") in place of LXX φιμώσεις
1
3
.
Notes Hebrew/Greek Ambiguity / Variant Manuscript: Aageson observes that κημώσεις versus φiμώσεις is a recognized dialectal/manuscript variant reading in Greek Old Testament transmission
1
3
.
Disagrees with Another Scholar / Allegorical Interpretation: Aageson addresses interpretations that reduce Paul’s argument to pure allegory; he argues that Paul uses rabbinic-style qal wahomer (a fortiori) reasoning to apply a literal Mosaic command about livestock directly to human apostolic rights
1
unfold_less
2
5
.
11. B001-11: 1 Corinthians 10:7 / Exodus 32:6
Disagrees with Another Scholar: Aageson explicitly disagrees with Leonhard Goppelt’s view that 1 Corinthians 10:1–13 is fundamental historical-redemptive typology. Aageson argues that τύπος in 1 Corinthians 10:6, 11 functions parenetically as a "moral warning" or "instructive example" rather than a formal typological scheme requiring historical escalation
1
unfold_less
2
5
.
Allows Authorial Adaptation / Midrashic Application: Aageson details how Paul selects Exodus 32:6 ("the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play") to provide midrashic parenetic instruction warning Corinthian believers against participating in pagan sacrificial feasts
1
3
.
12. B001-12: Galatians 3:13 / Deuteronomy 21:23
Discusses Competing Textual Form & Authorial Omission: Aageson emphasizes that Galatians 3:13 (Ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου) omits the divine agency phrase ὑπὸ θεοῦ from LXX Deuteronomy 21:23 (κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ θεοῦ)
1
unfold_less
3
4
.
Expresses Uncertainty / Allows Pre-Pauline Oral or Traditional Form: Aageson expresses uncertainty regarding the origin of the omission, stating: "Although we cannot be certain that Paul was first responsible for the omission of these words [ὑπὸ θεοῦ], it is likely that they were omitted in order to avoid presenting an unacceptable image of the divine. Paul, for his part, would not have wanted to risk implying that Christ was accursed by God"
1
3
.
Notes Lexical Adaptation: Aageson notes Paul’s lexical substitution of the adjective ἐπικατάρατος for the LXX participle κεκατηραμένος
1
3
.

Furthermore, we have sought to show that some of Paul's citations bear evidence of Hebrew influence. It has been argued also that five categories of textual variations can be discerned in Paul's scriptural quotations: 1) those involving articles, particles, conjunctions, pronouns, and prepositions; 2) those exhibiting different word order; 3) those reflecting variant word forms; 4) those involving the omission, addition, or substitution of words; and 5) those resulting from a paraphrastic manner of quoting. In addition, it has been argued that the double citations reflect some of the same types of variations between the two occurrences in the epistles as have been found between the LXX and the Pauline quotations. Within these five categories, a significant number of variations appear to have been the result of intentional modification of the scriptural text. Although the possibility cannot be ruled out that Paul in some cases may have quoted from memory, it seems evident that many variations are the consequence of an attempt to conform the text of scripture to the context of the epistles. As gleaned from our discussion in this chapter, these modifications may be classified as follows: 1) stylistic modifica­ tions, 2) literary variations designed to introduce the text or to allow it to fit smoothly and meaningfully into the epistolary context, 3) modifications designed to achieve a desired rhetorical effect, 4) changes which reflect a shift in historical perspective, 5) variations resulting from the universalization of particular scriptural statements, 6) manipulation of the text in order to support and enhance an argument, and 7) adaptation of the text for the purpose of avoiding an unacceptable theological/christological idea.

In chapter five, it has been indicated that the christological material in Romans 1:1-7, 3:21-26, and I Corinthians 15:3-4 has not been developed exegetically by Paul although reference to the scriptures is made in each of these texts. It has been argued also that in Romans 1:2, 3:21, and Galatians 3:8 the temporal and prospective dimension of Paul's understanding of scripture is exhibited. It has been shown in our examination of II Corinthians 3:4-4:6, I Corinthians 2:7-10, Romans 16:25-27, and 1:17 that Paul claimed special religious "insight" for himself and for those who share his faith in Christ and that this has shaped his view of scripture. Furthermore, Paul's application of scripture, it has been asserted, is characterized by two dimensions: 1) it is applied in order to illustrate and establish a religious principle and 2) it is applied to persons or things in the contemporary situation. It has been shown that certain citations have been applied explicitly, whereas others appear to have functioned as a source from which Paul has drawn a religious implication, idea, or consequence. It has also been shown that Paul understood scripture as a source of instruction and guidance. In addition, we have made the claim that typology, understood in terms of historical linkage, is limited in the epistles of Paul and is not an adequate term to describe the framework with which he approached the use of scripture. To identify and describe the connection between scriptural persons or things and contemporary persons or things, we have argued for the use of the term "correspondence" There is also evidence that Paul has used scripture allegorically. In the concluding section of chapter five, we have provided a comparison of Pauline and Jewish uses of scripture as this material has been presented in parts I and II of our thesis.
